title: DELETE did not shrink the table
hook: Why does a table keep growing after DELETE, and how do you tune autovacuum?

scenes.caption: DELETE leaves row versions that cannot always be reclaimed immediately.
scenes.narration: After deleting many rows, the table file remains large. PostgreSQL keeps obsolete versions until safe cleanup; normal vacuum generally makes that space reusable inside the relation.

items: Size alone does not prove a leak
Old snapshots may still need versions

scenes.caption: Dead-tuple estimates and vacuum history help explain growth.
scenes.narration: Inspect estimated dead tuples and recent autovacuum activity. These counters are clues, not an exact bloat measurement; compare them over time with transaction age and workload.

elements.text:
SELECT n_dead_tup,
       last_autovacuum,
       autovacuum_count
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname = 'orders';

items: Check long transactions and replication slots
Cleanup must respect the visibility horizon

scenes.caption: Large busy tables may need vacuum to start earlier.
scenes.narration: When cleanup is falling behind, investigate blockers and vacuum capacity first. This example lowers a table's scale factor; the right setting depends on its churn.

items: Thresholds are only part of scheduling

scenes.caption: VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and takes an exclusive lock.
scenes.narration: Run ordinary vacuum to reclaim reusable space. Vacuum full can shrink the file through a rewrite, but needs extra disk space and an exclusive lock.

items: Prefer reuse when future inserts need space
Plan downtime before a blocking rewrite

takeaway: Vacuum makes dead space reusable; investigate cleanup blockers before tuning thresholds or rewriting a table.
